title: Dynamic Slab Allocator for Sharded Weights and Preemption Guidelines
body:
Purpose and scope:

This doc describes a proposal for a Dynamic Slab Allocator (DSA) for sharded model weights aimed at optimizing GPU memory utilization, reducing cold-start latency, and providing a deterministic preemption path when memory pressure requires immediate reclamation. The DSA is intentionally orthogonal to the existing KV-cache eviction and batching systems; it focuses on how model weight bytes are mapped into GPU resident regions, how those regions are resized and migrated, and how we safely hot-swap or evict shards while respecting running inference requests.

Motivation / pain points:
- Current weight residency approaches operate at coarse shard/file granularity. For large sharded models the atomic unit is often a whole layer/tensor file which leads to fragmentation and high variance in eviction cost.
- Cold-starts and on-the-fly model switches cause large allocation spikes. We lack a graceful strategy to partially serve requests while streaming in remaining pieces.
- Multi-tenant hosts with mixed model footprints suffer from noisy neighbor evictions that produce unpredictable tail latency.
- Hot-swap/rollout workflows require a clear, safe protocol for swapping weight variants (FP16 vs quantized) without violating KV cache or execution state.

Design goals:
1) Fine-grained residency: allocate GPU memory in slabs (configurable slab_size, e.g., 32–64MB) rather than whole-file units so large tensors are composed of multiple slabs that can be independently resident and evicted.
2) Bounded allocation and fragmentation control: keep a small set of free slab sizes and a fast freelist to avoid runaway fragmentation.
3) Latency-safe preemption: support O(1) preemption of least-recently/least-critical slabs to free targeted memory within a deterministic timeframe.
4) Progressive activation: allow inference engine to execute on partially-resident model by stubbing absent slabs and filling with placeholder fused operators that trigger blocking fetch or use graceful degradation fallbacks.
5) Hot-swap safety: provide a 3-phase swap protocol (stage, commit, retire) to switch between weight variants with rollback support.

Key concepts and terminology:
- slab: contiguous GPU memory region sized to slab_size used to store a slice of a tensor shard.
- slab-id: unique identifier for a slab; maps to (model_id, shard_id, byte_offset).
- residency map: fast lookup table at runtime mapping slab-id -> resident (GPU ptr) | pending | remote (file path).
- anchor slab: a small set of always-resident slabs per model required for request entrypoints (embedding tables, initial LN layers).

Allocation policy:
- On model load, tensors are mapped into logical slabs. We do not immediately allocate all slabs to GPU. Instead we calculate an allocation budget per model instance based on tier (hosted/dedicated/private), SLA, and historical throughput.
- Slab freelist is separated into size-classes (powers-of-two multiples of base_slab), but the allocator prefers exact-size slabs where possible to reduce fragmentation.
- Heuristics for eager allocation: slabs that are anchor slabs, slabs for the first N decoder layers when average request length > threshold, and slabs referenced by pinned routes are prioritized.

Eviction and preemption:
- Eviction is performed at slab granularity. Each slab has metadata: last_used_ts, hotness_score (moving average of accesses weighted by sequence length), pinned_until (optional), and residency_cost (bytes + memory-locality score).
- Preemption mode: when memory pressure crosses a high watermark, the allocator first attempts cooperative eviction (background async writeback/unmap) of low hotness_score slabs. If free memory target not reached within preemption_timeout_ms, system enters deterministic preemption: sequentially unmap slabs from an ordered priority queue until target achieved.
- Deterministic preemption ensures we can promise to free X MB within Y ms which is critical for admission decisions on new large model attach requests.

Serving while partially resident (progressive activation):
- Stubbing: the execution engine must tolerate absent slabs by providing either:
  a) blocking fetch: the operator issues a fetch and stalls the op until slab is resident (incurs latency but preserves correctness), or
  b) graceful degrade: the operator substitutes a lower-fidelity quantized micro-kernel temporarily (if available), or
  c) fallback model: route request to a smaller variant that is fully resident (policy-based).
- For path (a), we prioritize fetching anchor slabs and decode layers first so initial tokens can stream while deeper layers load in background. This supports streaming tokens earlier even with partially loaded deep layers.

MMAP vs staged streaming strategy:
- Primary storage: safetensors files on remote or local cache with accompanying checksums and slab manifest (precomputed offsets matching slab boundaries).
- MMAP path: when storing weights on a local disk tier (NVMe) we try to mmap the safetensors region and promote slab pages to device memory via cudaMemcpyAsync into slab allocations. MMAP reduces copy overhead for cold read but requires robust page-fault handling in presence of preemption.
- Streaming path: for remote objects (object store), implement a slab-aware range fetcher that can request multiple parallel ranges with adaptive concurrency based on measured throughput. Use progressive integrity checks per slab (checksums).

Hot-swap protocol (3-phase):
1) Stage: load new variant slabs into an isolated slab pool and run validation hooks (sanity checks, sample evals on lightweight prompts). New slabs are marked staged and not visible to running requests.
2) Commit: atomically flip residency map pointers for anchor slabs first, then incrementally for remaining slabs. Commit is idempotent and recorded in a small on-disk commit-log to allow crash recovery. During commit, older slabs remain resident until the new slab is activated for each tensor slice.
3) Retire: background unmap and free of retired slab pool once no active request references old slab ids. A garbage collector runs with a grace period equal to max_inflight_request_latency.
- Rollback: if validation fails, the commit is aborted and staged slabs unmapped. We must ensure this path does not leak memory or leave half-committed pointers.

Concurrency and safety considerations:
- Per-slab reference counting: each inference execution that reads a slab increases its refcount; preemption cannot unmap slabs with refcount>0. Deterministic preemption therefore targets slabs with refcount==0 first; if insufficient, the admission controller can reject new incoming requests or route to other capacity tiers.
- Atomic pointer swaps: residency map flips must be performed with atomic writes (64-bit pointers or tagged pointers) to avoid torn reads by execution threads.
- Checkpointing: commit-log ensures that on process restart the allocator can reconcile which slab pools (staged/active/retired) are consistent.

Metrics and observability:
- slab_faults_per_minute, avg_fetch_latency_ms_per_slab, preemption_events_total, bytes_freed_per_preemption, anchor_slab_miss_ratio, staged_commit_duration_ms.
- Expose a per-model residency heatmap (slab id -> hotness_score) in the console to aid troubleshooting and to drive Optimize suggestions.

Rollout plan / implementation phases:
- Phase 0 (spike): implement slab manifest generation in model import path and a user-space allocator prototype (no preemption) used only in dev hosts.
- Phase 1 (alpha): integrate slab freelist, eviction heuristics, and streaming range fetcher. Add promotion hooks to scheduler to prefer anchor slabs.
- Phase 2 (beta): deterministic preemption + atomic commit-log for hot-swap. Start enabling for dedicated hosts behind a feature flag.
- Phase 3 (GA): enable for hosted fleet after extensive chaos testing, expose console metrics and controls for slab_size and preemption thresholds.

Open questions / trade-offs:
- slab_size selection: smaller slabs reduce eviction granularity but increase metadata and freelist pressure. Empirical tuning required per-model-family.
- refcount vs soft-pinning: maintaining strict refcounts prevents unsafe preemption but may lead to inability to reclaim memory under adversarial workloads. Need a hybrid approach with admission control.
- mmap semantics across kernels: page-in costs are non-deterministic on some kernels; we may combine mmap for NVMe warm caches and explicit async device copies for guaranteed timelines.

Short TODOs:
- Add unit tests for atomic commit/rollback.
- Add sim harness to replay request traces and measure bytes-freed targets vs time.
- Draft console UI wireframes for residency heatmaps and per-model slab tuning knobs.

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally a middleware-level allocator concept. It can coexist with existing weight-loading components (mmap lazyloader, safetensors fallback) but aims to provide stronger guarantees for preemption and hot-swap.
- Looking for feedback on slab sizing heuristics and practicality of per-slab reference counting at 10M slabs/host scale.

References and related docs:
